voiceover: The first number you see quietly steers your guess.
visual: Big number flashes, then a guess meter

voiceover: Psychologists call it anchoring. In a classic study, people spun a wheel of numbers before answering.
visual: Spinning number wheel animation

voiceover: They estimated the share of African countries in the United Nations. The wheel's number was meaningless.
visual: Simple map icon with a question mark

voiceover: Yet people who saw a high number gave higher estimates than people who saw a low one.
visual: Two bars: high-anchor group vs low-anchor group

voiceover: Anchors work on prices, salaries and sale tags too. What's the last anchor that fooled you?
visual: Price tag with a crossed-out number

voiceover: You know the word. It just won't come out.
visual: On-screen text: blank word with a blinking cursor
caption_pause: Big card: IT WON’T COME OUT

voiceover: That's the tip-of-the-tongue state. In a 1966 study, researchers read out definitions of rare words.
visual: Dictionary icon, definition text appears

voiceover: When people got stuck, they could often guess the first letter and how many syllables it had.
visual: Letter tiles: first letter lit, rest grey

voiceover: So the memory seems to be there. Your brain has the outline but can't reach the full sound.
visual: Simple diagram: word outline, sound missing

voiceover: It often pops back later on its own. Which word keeps escaping you?
visual: Text: “Which word?” with a comment bubble

voiceover: Say the color of each word out loud. Go.
visual: On-screen test: RED, BLUE, GREEN in mismatched ink

voiceover: Harder than it looked? Reading is so automatic the word fights the color you name.
visual: Same list, the word and ink pulling apart

voiceover: This is the Stroop effect, published in 1935. People named ink colors more slowly when the word clashed.
visual: Simple chart: matching vs clashing words, time bars

voiceover: It has been repeated in many labs, and researchers still use it to study attention.
visual: Lab icons and an attention meter

voiceover: Try the list again, slower. Which color tripped you up?
visual: The list again with a stopwatch icon

voiceover: The famous drooling-dog bell? It may never have rung.
visual: Animated bell icon with a question mark

voiceover: Around 1900, a Russian physiologist studying digestion saw his dogs drool before food even arrived.
visual: Simple drawing: dog, food bowl, lab coat

voiceover: They had linked the lab sounds and the helpers with dinner. Later, a sound alone made them drool.
visual: Diagram: sound + food → sound alone

voiceover: That's classical conditioning. His writings mention metronomes and buzzers; whether a bell was used is debated.
visual: Metronome and buzzer icons, bell greyed out

voiceover: The learning part is real. What sound makes your pet come running?
visual: Your pet reacting to a familiar sound

voiceover: The box already ticked for you is powerful.
visual: Animated checkbox ticking itself

voiceover: It's called the default effect. People tend to stick with whatever option is set unless they act.
visual: Toggle switch icons, most left as set

voiceover: A 2003 study compared European countries on organ donation, where you either opt in or opt out.
visual: Simple Europe outline with two colors

voiceover: Countries where donation was the default had far higher consent rates than countries where you had to tick.
visual: Two bars: opt-out countries vs opt-in countries

voiceover: Same choice, different starting point. Which default have you never changed?
visual: Phone settings screen mockup, toggles highlighted

voiceover: You didn't like that song. Now you hum it.
visual: Animated music note icon, thumbs down turning up

voiceover: Psychologists call this the mere exposure effect: just seeing something again can make you like it more.
visual: Repeating icon appearing again and again

voiceover: In a 1968 study, people saw unfamiliar foreign words and characters different numbers of times.
visual: On-screen made-up symbols repeated

voiceover: The more often they'd seen one, the more positive they guessed its meaning was.
visual: Rating scale sliding toward “good”

voiceover: It has limits: too much repetition can backfire. What grew on you over time?
visual: Repeat counter ticking up, then a frown

voiceover: You wake up, but your body won't move.
visual: Simple drawing: bed, eyes open, body outline still

voiceover: That's sleep paralysis. During dream sleep, most muscles go still so you don't act out dreams.
visual: Sleep stage diagram, dream stage highlighted

voiceover: Sometimes your mind wakes up a few seconds before that stillness switches off. You're aware but can't move.
visual: Two timelines: mind awake, muscles still asleep

voiceover: It can feel scary, and some people see or sense things. It usually passes within seconds or minutes.
visual: Soft clock icon, seconds ticking by

voiceover: It's common. Have you ever woken up unable to move?
visual: Calm sunrise graphic with comment bubble

voiceover: The ten percent brain claim? It's a myth.
visual: Brain outline with “10%” stamped, then crossed out

voiceover: It's in movies and ads, but no known study found most of the brain sitting idle.
visual: Movie-ticket and ad icons, generic and unbranded

voiceover: Brain scans show activity across the whole brain over a day, even during sleep.
visual: Brain outline lighting up in many areas

voiceover: Damage to almost any area can cause problems. That wouldn't happen if most of it were spare.
visual: Simple diagram: brain areas labeled by function

voiceover: Your brain is busy, not ninety percent asleep. Which brain myth did you believe?
visual: Busy brain icon with comment bubble

voiceover: You think everyone noticed. They mostly didn't.
visual: Spotlight icon on a stick figure

voiceover: This is the spotlight effect: we overestimate how much other people notice our looks and slips.
visual: Crowd icons, most looking at their phones

voiceover: In a 2000 study, students walked into a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt.
visual: Simple drawing: door, plain T-shirt with a big “?”

voiceover: They guessed about half the room noticed it. In that study, only about a quarter actually did.
visual: Two bars: guessed about half vs about a quarter

voiceover: You're the star of your own movie, not theirs. What moment still makes you cringe?
visual: Movie clapperboard icon, comment bubble

voiceover: You walk into a room and forget why.
visual: Simple drawing: person stops in a doorway, “?” above
caption_pause: Big card: WHY AM I HERE?

voiceover: Some researchers think doorways act like event boundaries, so your brain files the last room away.
visual: Animated folder closing as a door shuts

voiceover: In lab studies from 2006, walking through a doorway led to more forgetting than crossing one room.
visual: Diagram: two rooms vs one long room

voiceover: But the effect is small, and later studies found it shows up only in some conditions.
visual: Small bar labeled “small effect”

voiceover: Going back to the first room may help. What did you forget today?
visual: Arrow leading back through the door

voiceover: Each eye has a hole in its vision.
visual: Eye outline with a small dark gap

voiceover: Where the optic nerve leaves the back of the eye, there are no light-sensing cells at all.
visual: Simple eye diagram, optic nerve labeled

voiceover: That's your blind spot. Your brain fills it in using the other eye and the surrounding scene.
visual: Gap filling in with background pattern

voiceover: Try it: close your left eye, stare at the cross, and move closer until the dot vanishes.
visual: On-screen test: cross on left, dot on right

voiceover: Your vision has edits you never notice. Did the dot disappear for you?
visual: Same test card held for viewers

voiceover: More people on the rope, less effort each.
visual: Animated rope with stick figures added one by one

voiceover: Over a century ago, an engineer found teams pulled less than their members' solo efforts added up.
visual: Bars: expected team total vs actual total

voiceover: In 1979, psychologists asked people to clap and shout as loud as they could, alone or in groups.
visual: Simple drawing: people clapping, sound waves

voiceover: Each person made less noise in a group, even when they only believed others were shouting with them.
visual: Headphones icon, sound meter dropping

voiceover: It's called social loafing. Have you carried a group project alone?
visual: Group chat mockup, one name doing tasks

voiceover: That middle option might be there to steer you.
visual: Three menu cards, middle one glowing
caption_pause: Big card: WHY IS IT THERE?

voiceover: It's the decoy effect: a worse option can make another one look like a bargain.
visual: Scale tipping toward one option

voiceover: Picture small popcorn, a medium priced just under the large, and the large itself.
visual: Simple popcorn tubs: small, medium, large, no prices

voiceover: Next to that medium, the large looks smart. A classic 1982 study described this pull on choices.
visual: Arrow from medium to large, “smart pick” label

voiceover: The same pattern can appear in subscription plans. Which plan nudged you lately?
visual: Three generic plan cards, unbranded

voiceover: Ten nice comments. One mean one. Guess which sticks?
visual: Mock comment list: ten hearts, one red comment

voiceover: Psychologists call it negativity bias: bad events tend to grab more attention and weight than good ones.
visual: Scale tipping toward a small dark weight

voiceover: A well-known 2001 review gathered findings across relationships, feedback and memory pointing the same way.
visual: Stack of paper icons labeled with topics

voiceover: One idea is that noticing threats helped our ancestors survive, but that part is a theory.
visual: Simple campfire drawing with a “theory” label

voiceover: Knowing the bias can help you weigh feedback fairly. Which comment still lives in your head?
visual: Comment bubble icons, one glowing

voiceover: Your body clock isn't set to exactly 24 hours.
visual: Clock face icon with hands slightly past 12

voiceover: It's called your circadian rhythm, from Latin for about a day.
visual: Text: circa + dies = about a day

voiceover: When people live without clocks or daylight in labs, their rhythm drifts, running a little longer than 24 hours.
visual: Simple drawing: room with no window, clock crossed out

voiceover: Morning light helps reset it each day. That's partly why jet lag throws you off for days.
visual: Sunrise graphic, then a plane icon

voiceover: It also explains part of that afternoon slump. When do you feel most awake?
visual: Energy line dipping in the afternoon

voiceover: Left-brained or right-brained? Brain scans say neither.
visual: Brain outline split in two colors, then merging

voiceover: The popular idea says logical people use the left side and creative people use the right.
visual: Calculator icon left, paintbrush icon right

voiceover: Some functions do lean to one side. For most people, key language areas sit mainly on the left.
visual: Brain diagram, language area lightly marked left

voiceover: But a 2013 study of over a thousand brain scans found no sign of left-brained or right-brained people.
visual: Grid of many small brain icons, no split

voiceover: Both sides work together all day. Which label were you given?
visual: Both halves glowing together

voiceover: One good trait can paint your whole impression.
visual: Stick figure with a glowing halo

voiceover: That's the halo effect. It was named in 1920, when officers' ratings of soldiers moved together.
visual: Old-style rating sheet icon, 1920 label

voiceover: Soldiers rated high on physique tended to score high on intelligence and character too.
visual: Rating bars rising together

voiceover: Later studies found the same pull in job interviews, grading and first impressions of strangers.
visual: Icons: interview desk, graded paper, handshake

voiceover: One trait isn't the whole person. Who did you misjudge at first?
visual: Halo icon fading away

voiceover: Here are ten words. Which ones will you remember?
visual: On-screen list of ten simple words, one by one

voiceover: In list-learning studies, people tend to recall the first and last items best, not the middle.
visual: U-shaped recall curve drawing

voiceover: It's called the serial position effect. Early items get more rehearsal, and the last ones are still fresh.
visual: Curve labels: start = rehearsal, end = fresh

voiceover: In a 1966 study, a short delay before recall largely removed the end advantage, not the start.
visual: Clock icon, the curve's right end dropping

voiceover: Put key points first and last. Which of the ten did you remember?
visual: Slide outline: key point first and last

voiceover: That outlet is looking at you. Right?
visual: Your own close-up of a face-like wall outlet
caption_pause: Big card: IT’S LOOKING AT YOU

voiceover: Seeing faces in random objects is called face pareidolia, and it's very common.
visual: Your own photos: clouds, a car front, a bag

voiceover: Your brain is tuned to spot faces fast, so two dots and a line can be enough.
visual: Two dots and a line forming a face

voiceover: Brain-imaging studies suggest face-sensitive areas can respond to these objects too, not just to real faces.
visual: Simple brain outline, small area glowing

voiceover: It's normal, not a glitch. What's the funniest face you've spotted?
visual: Grid of your own face-like object photos

voiceover: Kids copy more than you think.
visual: Simple drawing: adult and child mirroring a pose

voiceover: In a 1961 study, preschoolers watched an adult hit and kick a large inflatable doll.
visual: Inflatable doll icon, adult silhouette

voiceover: Other children watched an adult play quietly, and some saw no adult at all.
visual: Two panels: quiet play vs empty room

voiceover: Later, kids who had seen the rough play were more likely to copy it, sometimes move for move.
visual: Child silhouette repeating the adult's pose

voiceover: It's called observational learning. What habit did you pick up by watching someone?
visual: Arrow from adult icon to child icon

voiceover: Paid for it, so you have to finish it?
visual: Movie ticket icon, yawning face emoji

voiceover: That's the sunk cost fallacy: sticking with something because of what you've already spent, not what's ahead.
visual: Coins falling into a pit labeled “spent”

voiceover: In a 1985 study, people imagined accidentally booking two ski trips for one weekend, a pricier and a cheaper one.
visual: Two simple trip cards, one marked pricier

voiceover: They were told they'd enjoy the cheaper trip more. Many still picked the pricier one, because more money was at stake.
visual: Pricier card chosen, smile on the cheaper card

voiceover: The money was gone either way. Only the future enjoyment was still a choice.
visual: Empty wallet icon, arrow pointing forward

voiceover: Next time, ask: would I start this today? What did you finish only because you paid?
visual: Text: “Would I start this today?”

voiceover: Punching a pillow to let anger out? Not quite.
visual: Animated pillow with a fist icon, then a “?”

voiceover: The idea is called catharsis: anger builds like steam, and venting it releases the pressure.
visual: Steam-kettle drawing with a pressure gauge

voiceover: In a 2002 study, people were made angry, then some hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them.
visual: Punching bag icon, thought bubble with a face outline

voiceover: Afterward, they felt angrier and acted more aggressively than people who simply sat quietly for a couple of minutes.
visual: Two bars: bag group angrier vs quiet group

voiceover: Venting seemed to rehearse the anger. In that study, doing nothing at all worked better.
visual: Loop arrow labeled “rehearse”

voiceover: So hitting things isn't a release valve. What helps you cool down?
visual: Calm wave graphic, comment bubble

voiceover: While you dream, your eyes are probably darting around.
visual: Closed eyelids drawing, small arrows darting

voiceover: In 1953, two researchers watching sleepers noticed bursts of fast eye movements under closed eyelids.
visual: Vintage-style lab icon, wires to a sleeper outline

voiceover: They called it rapid eye movement sleep, or REM. Brain activity during REM looked a lot like being awake.
visual: Two brain-wave lines: REM and awake, similar

voiceover: When sleepers were woken during REM, they reported vivid dreams far more often than when woken at other times.
visual: Dream bubble growing when an alarm icon rings

voiceover: Later research showed we cycle into REM several times a night, with longer REM periods toward morning.
visual: Sleep-cycle staircase chart across one night

voiceover: Dreams can happen outside REM too, often less vivid. Do you remember last night's dream?
visual: Dream bubble fading at sunrise

voiceover: Mozart for babies? The study wasn't even about babies.
visual: Baby-mobile icon with music notes, then a “?”

voiceover: In 1993, college students who listened to a Mozart sonata did slightly better on a spatial puzzle task.
visual: Simple paper-folding puzzle diagram

voiceover: The boost was small and lasted only around ten to fifteen minutes. It didn't measure general intelligence.
visual: Timer icon: ten to fifteen minutes

voiceover: Still, the idea spread fast, and products promising smarter babies followed.
visual: Generic unbranded product boxes with music notes

voiceover: Other labs struggled to repeat it, and big reviews found the effect small at best, maybe just extra alertness.
visual: Bar chart: original bar tall, repeats small

voiceover: Play music because you enjoy it, not as a brain upgrade. What song gets you focused?
visual: Headphones icon, comment bubble

voiceover: Here's 2, 4, 6. Guess my rule.
visual: Big on-screen numbers: 2, 4, 6

voiceover: In a 1960 study, people could test any three numbers to find the rule, then announce their guess.
visual: Notepad icon with blank number slots

voiceover: Many guessed something like 'goes up by two' and tested 8, 10, 12. Yes. Then 20, 22, 24. Yes.
visual: Number triples appearing with green YES ticks

voiceover: The real rule was any three rising numbers. People mostly tested examples that fit their idea, not ones that could break it.
visual: Rule card flips: “any three rising numbers”

voiceover: That's confirmation bias: looking for evidence that agrees with you and skipping what might prove you wrong.
visual: Magnifier passing over only green ticks

voiceover: A test like 10, 9, 8 would have helped. What belief have you never tried to disprove?
visual: Triple 10, 9, 8 with a red NO

voiceover: Cramming works. For about a day.
visual: Clock at 3 a.m., open book, coffee cup
caption_pause: Big card: FOR ABOUT A DAY

voiceover: In the 1880s, a German researcher memorized lists of nonsense syllables to measure how fast he forgot.
visual: Notebook with nonsense syllables like “DAX” and “BOK”

voiceover: He found forgetting is steep at first, then slows down. That curve is now called the forgetting curve.
visual: Forgetting curve drawing, steep then flat

voiceover: He also noticed that spreading practice over several days took fewer total repetitions than packing it into one sitting.
visual: Calendar: one crammed day vs several spaced days

voiceover: That's the spacing effect, and a large 2006 review of hundreds of studies backed it up.
visual: Stack of paper icons labeled “hundreds of studies”

voiceover: Same hours, spread out, tend to last longer. What are you cramming for right now?
visual: Two curves: cram fades, spaced stays higher

voiceover: Which line is longer? Look closely.
visual: Optical-illusion graphic: two lines with arrow fins

voiceover: They're the same length. This is the Müller-Lyer illusion, first published in 1889.
visual: Ruler slides in, lines shown equal

voiceover: The only difference is the arrow tips: fins pointing outward make a line look longer, fins pointing inward make it shorter.
visual: Fins highlighted: outward vs inward

voiceover: Even when you know the trick, the illusion doesn't go away. Knowing and seeing are handled differently.
visual: Ruler removed, illusion returns

voiceover: Why it happens is still debated. One idea is that the fins look like corners of rooms and buildings, which hint at distance.
visual: Simple drawing: room corner and building corner

voiceover: Measure the lines yourself. Did your eyes or your ruler win?
visual: Ruler on screen, comment bubble

voiceover: More people watching can mean less help. Sometimes.
visual: Crowd of simple figures, one hand raised

voiceover: In a 1968 study, students talked over an intercom and heard another student seem to have a seizure.
visual: Intercom icon with sound waves

voiceover: Students who thought they were the only listener helped far more often, and faster, than those who thought others were listening too.
visual: Two bars: alone helped more vs group

voiceover: This is the bystander effect. One explanation is diffusion of responsibility: each person assumes someone else will act.
visual: Responsibility arrow splitting among figures

voiceover: But a 2020 study of real street-camera footage found that someone stepped in during most public conflicts.
visual: Street-camera icon, many hands reaching in

voiceover: The lab effect is real, but crowds aren't hopeless. Would you step in first?
visual: One figure stepping forward, comment bubble

voiceover: Owning a mug can make it feel pricier.
visual: Plain mug on a table, price tag appearing

voiceover: In a 1990 study, some students were given a university coffee mug. Others were not.
visual: Simple drawing: classroom, half the desks with mugs

voiceover: Mug owners were asked their lowest selling price. The others were asked the most they'd pay to buy one.
visual: Two price tags: sell price vs buy price

voiceover: Sellers asked for roughly twice what buyers would offer, for the very same mug they'd had for minutes.
visual: Sell tag grows to about twice the buy tag

voiceover: It's called the endowment effect. Owning something seems to make giving it up feel like a loss.
visual: Hand holding the mug, “loss” label

voiceover: Its size varies by situation, but it shows up a lot. What would you never sell?
visual: Yard-sale table icons, comment bubble

voiceover: Would you pick more discomfort, if it ended gently?
visual: Thermometer icon dropping, question mark

voiceover: In a 1993 study, people held one hand in very cold water for sixty seconds.
visual: Simple drawing: hand above a water bowl, timer 60

voiceover: In another trial, they did the same sixty seconds, then thirty more while the water warmed slightly.
visual: Timer 60 + 30, water color slightly warming

voiceover: Asked which trial to repeat, most chose the longer one: more total discomfort, but a gentler ending.
visual: Two trial cards, longer one ticked

voiceover: This is the peak-end rule: we tend to judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and how it ends.
visual: Line graph: peak marked, end marked

voiceover: Length matters less than you'd think. What ending made a whole trip for you?
visual: Suitcase icon with a glowing final day

voiceover: Dreams last seconds? Lab studies suggest otherwise.
visual: Dream bubble with a stopwatch icon

voiceover: A popular idea says a whole dream flashes by in the moment before you wake up.
visual: Flash animation inside a dream bubble

voiceover: In a 1957 study, sleepers were woken either five or fifteen minutes into dream sleep and asked which it had been.
visual: Clock icons: 5 min and 15 min

voiceover: They chose correctly most of the time, and longer dream sleep came with longer, more detailed dream reports.
visual: Two dream reports: short note vs long page

voiceover: So dreams seem to unfold in something close to real time, not a split-second flash.
visual: Timeline: dream unfolding minute by minute

voiceover: The memory is what fades fast once you wake. How long did your last dream feel?
visual: Dream bubble fading, comment bubble

voiceover: Visual learner? The evidence doesn't back the label.
visual: Quiz result card stamped “VISUAL LEARNER”

voiceover: The idea: everyone has a learning style, visual, auditory or hands-on, and learns best when taught that way.
visual: Three icons: eye, ear, hand

voiceover: People do have preferences. But the real test is whether matching teaching to your style improves what you learn.
visual: Two-path diagram: matched vs mismatched lesson

voiceover: A 2008 review looked for studies built to test exactly that, and found very few, with little support among them.
visual: Magnifier over a thin stack of papers

voiceover: Later experiments that did test it mostly found no benefit from matching lessons to a person's style.
visual: Two equal bars: matched vs mismatched

voiceover: Better-supported ideas: pictures plus words for everyone, and quizzing yourself. Which style were you told you had?
visual: Picture-plus-words card, quiz card

voiceover: Guess: more words with K first, or third?
visual: Big letter K in positions 1 and 3
caption_pause: Big card: K FIRST OR THIRD?

voiceover: In a 1973 study, most people guessed K first. In typical English text, K third is actually more common.
visual: Bars: guessed K first vs actual K third

voiceover: Words starting with K are easier to pull from memory, so they feel more common. That's the availability heuristic.
visual: Memory drawer opening, K words popping out

voiceover: We tend to judge how often something happens by how easily examples come to mind, and vivid stories come to mind fast.
visual: Thought bubble filling with vivid headline icons

voiceover: That's one reason plane crashes can feel more likely than car crashes, even though, mile for mile, driving is riskier.
visual: Plane and car icons, risk scale

voiceover: When something feels common, ask if it's just memorable. What risk do you overestimate?
visual: Question mark over a dramatic headline icon

voiceover: Seven, plus or minus two. Maybe fewer.
visual: Big number 7 with ± 2, then a “?”

voiceover: In 1956, a famous paper noted people can hold about seven items in mind, give or take two.
visual: Seven dots in a row, two fading

voiceover: That paper also described chunking: grouping items so 1-9-1-4 becomes one year, 1914, instead of four digits.
visual: Digits 1 9 1 4 snapping into “1914”

voiceover: Later researchers argued the true limit is smaller. A 2001 review put it closer to four chunks.
visual: Four boxes labeled “chunks”

voiceover: The exact number is still debated, and it depends on what you're remembering and whether you can rehearse.
visual: Scale with “words”, “digits”, “faces” weights

voiceover: Either way, chunking helps: phone numbers come in groups for a reason. How many digits can you hold?
visual: Phone number split into groups

voiceover: Loud room, ten conversations. Your name cuts through.
visual: Crowd icons with speech bubbles, one name glowing

voiceover: In 1953, a researcher studied how people follow one voice among many. He called it the cocktail party problem.
visual: Many sound waves, one highlighted

voiceover: People wore headphones with a different message in each ear and repeated just one aloud.
visual: Headphones diagram: left message, right message

voiceover: Afterward, they could say almost nothing about the ignored message, not even when its language changed.
visual: Ignored-ear side greyed out

voiceover: But in a 1959 follow-up, about a third of people noticed when their own name was slipped into the ignored ear.
visual: Name tag popping into the grey side

voiceover: Your brain seems to keep a quiet ear on the noise for things that matter to you. What word makes you turn around?
visual: Ear icon with a filter funnel

voiceover: Paid less to lie, they believed it more.
visual: Two coin stacks, small one glowing
caption_pause: Big card: PAID LESS, BELIEVED MORE

voiceover: In a 1959 study, students spent an hour on painfully boring tasks, like turning pegs on a board.
visual: Peg-board drawing, pegs turning, clock icon

voiceover: Then they were paid to tell the next student the tasks were fun. Some got a tiny payment, others twenty times more.
visual: Two envelopes: tiny vs twenty times bigger

voiceover: Later, the students paid the tiny amount rated the boring tasks as more enjoyable than those paid well.
visual: Rating bars: tiny-pay group higher

voiceover: The classic explanation: cognitive dissonance. A big payment justified the lie. A tiny one didn't, so their opinion shifted instead.
visual: Mind and action icons pulling apart, then aligning

voiceover: We sometimes bend beliefs to match what we've done. When did you talk yourself into something?
visual: Thought bubble rewriting itself

voiceover: Twenty-four jams on a table. Fewer sales?
visual: Table of many jam jars, unbranded

voiceover: In a 2000 study, a grocery store tasting booth showed either six jams or twenty-four.
visual: Two tables: six jars vs twenty-four

voiceover: The big display drew more people in, but far fewer of them bought a jar than shoppers at the small one.
visual: Two bars: visitors vs buyers per table

voiceover: The idea became famous as choice overload: too many options can leave people stuck and less satisfied.
visual: Person icon frozen before a long shelf

voiceover: But a 2010 review combining many studies found the average effect was close to zero. Some studies found it, some didn't.
visual: Many small study cards averaging to a flat line

voiceover: It seems to depend on things like how hard options are to compare. Do big menus stress you out?
visual: Two menus: easy to compare vs cluttered

voiceover: Was it a crush, or just a racing heart?
visual: Heart icon beating fast, question mark
caption_pause: Big card: CRUSH OR HEART RATE?

voiceover: In a 1974 study, a woman interviewed men on either a wobbly suspension bridge or a low, steady one.
visual: Two bridges: tall swaying one, low solid one

voiceover: She gave each man her phone number. More men from the wobbly bridge called her afterward.
visual: Phone icon ringing, tally favoring the wobbly bridge

voiceover: The idea: their pounding hearts came from the bridge, but some of that arousal got read as attraction.
visual: Heart arrow pointing to a bridge, then a person

voiceover: It's called misattribution of arousal. Later studies are mixed, and the original sample was small.
visual: Scale with mixed study cards

voiceover: So a scary movie date is no sure thing. Have you ever mixed up nerves and butterflies?
visual: Popcorn icon with a question mark

voiceover: Learn French while you sleep? Not quite.
visual: Pillow with headphones, floating word cards

voiceover: Old ads promised you could learn by playing recordings at night. It's called sleep learning, or hypnopedia.
visual: Old-style record player icon by a bed

voiceover: In a 1956 study, researchers played answers to questions during sleep, but checked brain waves to confirm people were truly asleep.
visual: Brain-wave line with a “sleep” label

voiceover: Answers played during real sleep weren't remembered. Earlier 'success' stories had likely caught people half awake.
visual: Quiz sheet with blank answers

voiceover: Newer studies suggest the sleeping brain can pick up very simple links between sounds or smells. That's a long way from vocabulary.
visual: Simple tone and scent icons linked by a line

voiceover: Sleep can help you keep what you studied while awake. Would you try sleep learning anyway?
visual: Book by the bed, sunrise

voiceover: Two minutes of power posing changes your hormones? No.
visual: Stick figure in a wide pose, hormone meter

voiceover: A 2010 study claimed that standing in expansive poses for two minutes raised testosterone and lowered stress hormones.
visual: Two-minute timer, arrows on two hormone bars

voiceover: It became hugely popular, with advice to strike a pose before interviews and big meetings.
visual: Generic stage and spotlight icons, no real talk

voiceover: In 2015, a larger study repeated it and found no hormone changes. Later reviews agreed the hormone claim didn't hold up.
visual: Original bar tall, larger study bar flat

voiceover: What may remain is smaller: some studies find people report feeling a bit more powerful after posing.
visual: Small mood meter nudging up slightly

voiceover: A feeling, not a hormone hack. Did you ever try a power pose before something big?
visual: Stick figure relaxing, comment bubble

voiceover: The Dunning-Kruger meme? The study said something different.
visual: Meme-style confidence curve, then a “?” stamp
caption_pause: Big card: NOT WHAT YOU THINK

voiceover: In 1999, students took tests of logic, grammar and humor, then guessed how well they'd done compared with others.
visual: Test paper icons: logic, grammar, humor

voiceover: The lowest scorers overestimated themselves the most. On average they placed themselves above the middle, while scoring near the bottom.
visual: Two bars per group: actual vs self-estimate

voiceover: Top scorers, meanwhile, slightly underestimated how they compared. That pattern became famous as the Dunning-Kruger effect.
visual: Top group bars: estimate slightly below actual

voiceover: But the memes exaggerate it. Low scorers didn't think they were experts. They still rated themselves lower than top scorers rated themselves.
visual: Bottom group's estimate bar below top group's

voiceover: And some researchers argue part of the pattern is a statistical artifact: noisy self-ratings plus a common habit of feeling above average.
visual: Scatter dots pulling toward the middle line

voiceover: So the effect is real but debated in size. It's not proof that people who disagree with you are clueless.
visual: Scale: real effect, debated size

voiceover: Where do you think you overrate yourself? Be honest below.
visual: Comment bubble with a mirror icon

voiceover: One word changed what people remembered seeing.
visual: Two speech bubbles: “hit” and “smashed”

voiceover: In a 1974 study, students watched short films of car crashes, then answered questions about them.
visual: Simple animated toy cars bumping, no injuries

voiceover: One group was asked how fast the cars were going when they 'hit' each other. Another heard 'smashed.'
visual: Question card with the verb swapping

voiceover: Same film, but the 'smashed' group gave higher speed estimates on average than the 'hit' group.
visual: Speedometer needle higher for “smashed”

voiceover: A week later, they were asked if they'd seen broken glass. There was none in the film.
visual: Calendar flips one week, glass icon with “?”

voiceover: People who heard 'smashed' were more likely to say yes. The question seemed to have changed the memory itself.
visual: Bar: more “yes” answers in the smashed group

voiceover: This is the misinformation effect. Memory isn't a recording. It's rebuilt each time, and new details can slip in.
visual: Memory puzzle rebuilding with a new piece

voiceover: Have you ever remembered something that turned out wrong?
visual: Comment bubble with a puzzle piece

voiceover: Count the passes. Don't lose track.
visual: Your own animated dots passing between two teams

voiceover: In a 1999 study, people watched a short video of two teams passing basketballs and counted one team's passes.
visual: Simple animation: two teams of colored dots passing

voiceover: Midway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle, faced the camera, and walked off.
visual: Gorilla icon walking across the animation

voiceover: About half of the viewers never noticed the gorilla at all. Some insisted it wasn't in the video.
visual: Pie chart: about half noticed, half didn't

voiceover: This is inattentional blindness: when your attention is locked on one task, unexpected things can go unseen.
visual: Spotlight narrowing on the passing dots

voiceover: Your eyes may point right at something, but without attention it may never reach your awareness.
visual: Eye icon with a closed gate to a brain

voiceover: It's one reason a hard count, a phone or a busy road can hide the obvious.
visual: Phone and road icons, gorilla icon faded

voiceover: Be honest: did you ever miss something this obvious?
visual: Gorilla icon waving, comment bubble

voiceover: Which line matches? Now everyone else says B.
visual: Line-matching card: one line, options A, B, C

voiceover: In the 1950s, students were asked to match a line to one of three others.
visual: Same card, clean and simple

voiceover: Alone, people almost never got it wrong. But in this test, everyone else in the room was secretly working with the researcher.
visual: Row of chairs, all but one marked with a star

voiceover: On many rounds, they all gave the same wrong answer out loud, before the real participant answered.
visual: Speech bubbles all saying “B”

voiceover: About a third of the answers on those rounds went along with the group. Roughly three in four people conformed at least once.
visual: Pie: about a third conformed answers

voiceover: But that also means most answers stayed correct, and about a quarter of people never gave in.
visual: Most answers ticked green

voiceover: When just one other person gave the right answer, conformity dropped sharply. One ally made a big difference.
visual: One chair glowing as an ally

voiceover: Would you have held your answer, or gone with the room?
visual: Card again, cursor hovering over answers

voiceover: Same facts, different words, opposite choice.
visual: Two cards: “200 saved” and “400 die”

voiceover: In 1981, two researchers asked people to imagine a disease outbreak expected to cost six hundred lives.
visual: Simple map icon with a warning symbol, number 600

voiceover: One group chose between plans described as lives saved: two hundred saved for sure, or a one-in-three chance to save everyone.
visual: Card A: sure save vs dice with 1/3

voiceover: Most picked the sure thing. Another group saw the same plans described as lives lost: four hundred die for sure, or the gamble.
visual: Same cards relabeled in red loss wording

voiceover: Now most picked the gamble. The outcomes were identical. Only the wording changed.
visual: Equals sign between the two card pairs

voiceover: This is the framing effect. Framed as gains, we tend to play safe; framed as losses, we gamble more.
visual: Two arrows: safe path vs gamble path

voiceover: You see it in ads too: ninety percent fat-free sounds better than ten percent fat.
visual: Generic food label with two wordings

voiceover: Which version would you have picked: safe, or the gamble?
visual: Two buttons: SAFE and GAMBLE

voiceover: Is a smile the same in every culture?
visual: Simple smiley drawing with a globe icon

voiceover: In the 1960s and 70s, researchers showed photos of facial expressions to people in many countries.
visual: Grid of simple drawn faces, no real photos

voiceover: In a 1971 study, people in a remote community in Papua New Guinea matched faces to short stories, like a friend arriving.
visual: Map outline, story card with a face to match

voiceover: They often matched them the way Westerners did, which suggested some basic expressions might be universal.
visual: Matching lines between faces and story cards

voiceover: That idea became textbook material: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust, read the same everywhere.
visual: Six simple drawn faces labeled by emotion

voiceover: But later work found the picture is messier. Accuracy drops when people get no list of emotion words to choose from.
visual: Answer list fading away, accuracy bar drops

voiceover: A large 2019 review argued people don't reliably show or read emotions from faces alone. Context matters a lot.
visual: Same face drawing, two different background scenes

voiceover: So some overlap, plenty of debate. Can you read your friends' faces without context?
visual: Face drawing with a question bubble

voiceover: Can you know you're dreaming, inside the dream?
visual: Dream cloud with a lightbulb inside
caption_pause: Big card: AWARE IN A DREAM?

voiceover: That's called lucid dreaming. For a long time, many scientists doubted it, because dream reports come after waking.
visual: Doubtful face icon next to a dream report

voiceover: Maybe people were just awake and imagining, or remembering wrongly. How do you test a dream from the inside?
visual: Two thought bubbles: awake vs asleep, “?”

voiceover: Here's the trick: your eye movements in dream sleep can follow where you look in the dream.
visual: Eye icon tracking a dot inside a dream cloud

voiceover: In early 1980s studies, sleepers agreed on a signal before bed: look left, right, left, right once they knew they were dreaming.
visual: Arrows: left, right, left, right

voiceover: Lab equipment showed them in dream sleep, and the agreed eye signal appeared right on cue.
visual: Signal trace with the eye pattern highlighted

voiceover: That's how lucid dreaming was confirmed in the lab. Many people report having one at least once.
visual: Lab checklist with a green tick

voiceover: Have you ever realized you were dreaming?
visual: Dream cloud with a comment bubble

voiceover: You've heard willpower runs out like a battery.
visual: Animated battery icon draining to red

voiceover: The idea is called ego depletion, and it started with a famous 1998 study.
visual: Old journal icon with a “1998” label

voiceover: People told to eat radishes instead of nearby cookies gave up sooner on an impossible puzzle afterward.
visual: Simple drawing: radish plate vs cookie plate

voiceover: Hundreds of follow-up studies seemed to agree, and the battery idea spread into self-help books and productivity advice.
visual: Stack of book icons growing

voiceover: Then labs tried something stricter. In 2016, one project ran a standard version in over twenty labs at once.
visual: Diagram: many lab icons light up together

voiceover: The result? An effect close to zero. A later multi-lab project also found, at most, a very small effect.
visual: Bar chart: tall original bar, tiny repeat bar

voiceover: Feeling tired is real. What didn't hold up is the simple fuel-tank story, and giving up likely has many causes.
visual: Fuel-gauge icon with a question mark

voiceover: Do you think willpower runs out? Tell me in the comments.
visual: Battery icon + comment bubble

voiceover: You knew it all along? Probably not.
visual: Crystal ball icon with a “?” stamp
caption_pause: Big card: KNEW IT ALL ALONG?

voiceover: Hindsight bias is the feeling, after something happens, that it was obvious and you saw it coming.
visual: Timeline: event happens, arrow loops backward

voiceover: In a 1975 study, people read about a historical battle. Some were told how it ended, others weren't.
visual: Old map icon, two outcome cards

voiceover: Those told an outcome rated it as more likely, whichever outcome they were told.
visual: Likelihood bars rising for the told outcome

voiceover: Worse, they tended to think they'd have predicted it anyway, and that others would have too.
visual: Thought bubble: “I knew it”

voiceover: Other studies found people misremember their own earlier predictions, shifting them toward what actually happened.
visual: Prediction note being rewritten with an eraser

voiceover: That makes it hard to learn from surprises. Writing predictions down before the result is one simple check.
visual: Sealed envelope labeled “prediction”

voiceover: What result did you swear you saw coming? Tell me in the comments.
visual: Notebook icon, comment bubble

voiceover: Rereading feels like learning. Often, it isn't.
visual: Highlighter moving over a page, sleepy face

voiceover: In a 2006 study, students read short prose passages, then either reread them or wrote down what they remembered.
visual: Two desks: reread icon vs blank notepad

voiceover: Tested five minutes later, the rereading group did a bit better. That may be why rereading feels like it works.
visual: Five-minute timer, reread bar slightly higher

voiceover: But tested a week later, the group that practiced recalling remembered clearly more than the group that reread.
visual: Calendar one week later, recall bar higher

voiceover: This is the testing effect, also called retrieval practice. Pulling information out of memory seems to strengthen it.
visual: Arrow pulling a card out of a brain icon

voiceover: It has been repeated across many ages, subjects and test types, which makes it one of learning research's sturdier findings.
visual: Grid of icons: kids, adults, subjects

voiceover: Easy ways to use it: flashcards, practice questions, or closing the book and writing what you remember.
visual: Flashcards and practice-question icons

voiceover: What are you studying right now? Try one recall round today.
visual: Notebook icon, comment bubble

voiceover: Mid-conversation, the stranger was swapped. Would you notice?
visual: Two simple figures, one fading into another

voiceover: In a 1998 study, a researcher stopped people on a college campus to ask for directions.
visual: Campus map icon, figure with a paper map

voiceover: Mid-conversation, two workers carried a door between them. Behind it, a different researcher took the first one's place.
visual: Door icon sliding between two figures

voiceover: The new person had different clothes, a different voice and a different height. The conversation simply continued.
visual: Side-by-side figures: clothes, height, voice icons

voiceover: About half of the people in that study never noticed they were now talking to someone else.
visual: Pie: about half noticed, half didn't

voiceover: This is change blindness. We keep far less detail from moment to moment than it feels like we do.
visual: Film strip with frames differing slightly

voiceover: Your brain seems to store the gist, like 'a person asking directions', and fills in the rest.
visual: Thought bubble with a simple sketch label

voiceover: Would you have noticed the swap? Be honest.
visual: Two figures, comment bubble

voiceover: Would you follow orders you thought were hurting someone?
visual: Simple dial graphic with a hand hovering

voiceover: In a 1963 study, volunteers were told to give a learner electric shocks for each wrong answer.
visual: Two desks, a wall between them, intercom icon

voiceover: The shocks weren't real, and the learner was an actor. But the volunteers believed the shocks were getting stronger.
visual: Dial graphic with an “actor” label on the far side

voiceover: When volunteers hesitated, a researcher calmly told them to continue. In the best-known version, about two in three went to the highest level.
visual: Pie chart: about two in three

voiceover: Many were visibly stressed and argued, which is part of why the study is now seen as an ethics lesson too.
visual: Worried face icon, ethics checklist

voiceover: But across later versions, obedience rates varied a lot, dropping sharply when the researcher gave orders by phone, for example.
visual: Bar chart: rates across versions, phone version low

voiceover: A partial repeat in 2009 found similar rates. What it all means about people is still debated.
visual: Two bars: 1963 vs 2009, question mark

voiceover: What do you think would make you stop?
visual: Stop sign icon, comment bubble

voiceover: Losses sting more than gains please. But how much?
visual: Plus and minus icons on a seesaw, minus heavier

voiceover: Picture a coin flip where tails costs you a set amount. How much would heads need to pay?
visual: Coin icon flipping: heads plus, tails minus

voiceover: In studies like this, many people turn the bet down unless the possible win is far bigger than the possible loss.
visual: Seesaw: small win side rejected, big win accepted

voiceover: In 1979, two psychologists built this into prospect theory. It's called loss aversion: a loss tends to weigh more than an equal gain.
visual: Curve graph: steeper on the loss side

voiceover: You'll often hear that losses hurt about twice as much. That number came from some early estimates, not a law of nature.
visual: Text “2x” stamped, then “about?”

voiceover: Later studies found the size changes a lot with the stakes, the situation and how the choice is asked.
visual: Dial labeled “size” turning with stakes

voiceover: Some researchers even argue that for small amounts, losses and gains can feel about equal. The debate is ongoing.
visual: Two even weights on the seesaw, small coins

voiceover: Do losses sting more for you than wins feel good?
visual: Seesaw icon, comment bubble

voiceover: Does a huge windfall make you happier for good?
visual: Confetti graphic slowly fading to grey

voiceover: Hedonic adaptation is the idea that after big changes, our mood tends to drift back toward its usual level.
visual: Mood line rising, then drifting back to baseline

voiceover: A famous 1978 study compared a small group of lottery winners with people who hadn't won.
visual: Two small groups of figure icons

voiceover: The winners weren't much happier, and they enjoyed everyday pleasures a little less. That result became famous.
visual: Two mood meters nearly level

voiceover: But that group was small. A large 2020 study of thousands of winners in Sweden found big wins raised life satisfaction for years.
visual: Large crowd of icons, satisfaction bar staying up

voiceover: Interestingly, day-to-day happiness and mood changed much less than overall life satisfaction did.
visual: Two bars: life satisfaction up, daily mood flat

voiceover: So adaptation is real, but it isn't the whole story. It depends on what changed and what you measure.
visual: Scale balancing two labels: “adapt” and “lasting”

voiceover: What exciting change wore off fastest for you?
visual: Calendar icon, comment bubble

voiceover: Study, then sleep. Your memory may thank you.
visual: Book resting on a pillow, moon icon

voiceover: In 1924, two psychologists had people learn nonsense syllables, then tested them hours later.
visual: Notebook with nonsense syllables, 1924 label

voiceover: Sometimes those hours were spent asleep. Other times, awake and going about a normal day.
visual: Split screen: moon side vs sun side

voiceover: After the same amount of time, they remembered more when they had slept. It was a tiny study, with just two participants.
visual: Two bars: slept higher, awake lower, “n = 2”

voiceover: Their idea was that being awake fills the day with new input that interferes with what you just learned.
visual: New icons crowding over a fresh memory

voiceover: Since then, many studies have backed the basic finding, and sleep now seems to do more than just protect memories.
visual: Stack of study icons growing

voiceover: During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay and strengthen new memories, a process called consolidation.
visual: Brain icon replaying a short film strip

voiceover: So an all-nighter may cost you more than sleep. When do you usually study?
visual: Moon icon, comment bubble

voiceover: One marshmallow now, or two if you wait?
visual: Two marshmallow icons and a kitchen timer

voiceover: In studies at a university preschool starting around 1970, kids could eat one treat now or wait for two.
visual: Simple drawing: child, plate, bell on a table

voiceover: Years later, follow-ups found kids who waited longer tended to have better test scores and other outcomes.
visual: Arrow from timer to graduation-cap icon

voiceover: That became a famous lesson: teach kids to wait and they'll succeed. But the original follow-up samples were small and not very diverse.
visual: Small group of icons, all alike

voiceover: In 2018, researchers repeated the idea with a much larger, more varied group of children.
visual: Large mixed group of icons

voiceover: The link with later achievement was about half as strong, and it shrank a lot once family background was taken into account.
visual: Bar halving, then shrinking further

voiceover: So waiting may partly reflect a child's circumstances, not just willpower. The test still says something, just less.
visual: Timer icon next to a house icon

voiceover: Would you have waited for the second treat?
visual: Marshmallow icons, comment bubble

voiceover: They're late, so they must be careless?
visual: Clock icon, figure running late

voiceover: Blaming someone's character and overlooking their situation has a name: the fundamental attribution error.
visual: Two arrows: character vs situation, one bolded

voiceover: In a 1967 study, students read essays either for or against a controversial foreign leader.
visual: Two essay sheets: “for” and “against”

voiceover: Some were told the writers chose their side. Others were told the writers had been assigned a side.
visual: Coin-toss icon labeled “assigned”

voiceover: Even when the side was assigned, readers still tended to judge the writers as believing what they wrote.
visual: Reader icon with a thought bubble over the essay

voiceover: We tend to read people's actions as personality and underweight the situation behind them.
visual: Spotlight on the person, situation in shadow

voiceover: The effect seems stronger in some cultures than others, but it shows up widely. Next time, ask what the situation was.
visual: Globe icon, then a situation checklist

voiceover: Who did you misjudge before you knew their whole situation?
visual: Figure with context panel revealed

voiceover: Your most vivid memories? Maybe not so accurate.
visual: Camera-flash graphic over a blank screen

voiceover: A flashbulb memory is a sharp, detailed memory of where you were when you heard shocking news.
visual: Photo-frame graphic with a blurred scene

voiceover: They feel like photographs. So psychologists tested them by asking people right after big news, then again months or years later.
visual: Two notepads: day one and years later

voiceover: In a 1992 study, students wrote down how they heard about a space shuttle disaster the day after it happened.
visual: Generic rocket icon, notepad with handwriting

voiceover: About two and a half years later, many of their new accounts differed sharply from what they had written.
visual: Two notes side by side, differences highlighted

voiceover: Yet many felt very confident, and some insisted their new version was right even when shown their own handwriting.
visual: Confidence meter at full, note with a cross

voiceover: A 2003 study found the same pattern: vivid memories faded like ordinary ones, but confidence stayed high.
visual: Two lines: accuracy falling, confidence flat

voiceover: What news moment do you remember vividly? Write it down today.
visual: Pen and notebook, comment bubble

voiceover: Listen with your eyes closed. Now open them.
visual: Animated mouth drawing, eyes-closed icon

voiceover: In a 1976 study, people watched a video of a face saying one sound while the audio played another.
visual: Animated mouth shaping a sound, audio wave below

voiceover: The audio said 'ba.' The lips formed 'ga.' Many people reported hearing a third sound: 'da.'
visual: Three cards: BA, GA, DA

voiceover: Close your eyes and the sound goes back to 'ba.' Open them, and for many people it changes again.
visual: Eye icon closing and opening

voiceover: This is the McGurk effect. It shows your brain blends what you see and hear into one experience.
visual: Eye and ear icons merging into one bubble

voiceover: Knowing the trick doesn't switch it off for many people. The illusion keeps working on repeat viewings.
visual: Repeat loop icon over the mouth drawing

voiceover: Not everyone experiences it, and strength varies by person and language. But it's a famous sign that hearing isn't just ears.
visual: Bar chart: effect strength varies by person

voiceover: What did you hear: ba, ga or da?
visual: Three answer buttons: BA, GA, DA

voiceover: The famous prison study? Its lesson is now disputed.
visual: Simple drawn icons: keys, bars, a question mark

voiceover: In 1971, students were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison in a university basement.
visual: Basement floor-plan drawing with two role badges

voiceover: Planned for two weeks, it was stopped after six days, as some guards treated prisoners harshly and prisoners grew distressed.
visual: Calendar: 14 days planned, stop sign at day 6

voiceover: The popular takeaway: give ordinary people a role and power, and they'll turn cruel on their own.
visual: Text card with the popular takeaway

voiceover: But it was one small study with no comparison group, and no close repeat has confirmed its conclusions.
visual: Diagram: one study, no comparison group

voiceover: Later reviews of recordings and archives suggest guards were encouraged to act tough, so the behavior wasn't purely spontaneous.
visual: Archive box and tape icons, magnifier

voiceover: A later prison study filmed for TV found guards didn't simply turn harsh. Many psychologists now treat the original as a cautionary tale.
visual: TV icon, scale tipping toward “disputed”

voiceover: What do you think: does power change people, or do roles?
visual: Two icons: crown and name badge, comment bubble
